page: Amazon Web Services m4.xlarge is a general-purpose, fourth-generation virtual server running on the Xen hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor. The instance is configured with 4 dedicated vCPUs, derived from 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled (2 threads per core). The CPU operates at a clock speed of 2.4 GHz and includes a 45 MB L3 cache. It supports AVX, AES, BMI2, and FMA instruction sets, but lacks AVX-512 extensions.

The instance is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced allocation of 4.0 GB per core. It does not include any bundled local storage or dedicated GPU hardware. Network connectivity is limited to a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps, and the instance does not come with complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations place the m4.xlarge in the lower performance tiers. In stress-ng CPU testing, both single-core (1282.39) and multi-core (3353.46) metrics fall within the bottom 25% of tested servers. Memory read-only bandwidth is measured at 177.74 GB/sec for cached small blocks and drops to 24.01 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. Database operations, such as Redis SET, achieve 1.44 million operations per second, which is in the bottom 10%. These results indicate a performance profile suited for legacy workloads or low-intensity tasks rather than modern, high-throughput applications.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m4.xlarge offers a stable, dedicated resource allocation but operates on older-generation hardware. This makes it less resource-dense and less computationally efficient compared to newer instance families. It is best utilized for general-purpose workloads with predictable, low-to-moderate resource demands, such as basic web serving, small development environments, or legacy application hosting.

It features 4 dedicated vCPUs (2 physical cores with hyper-threading), 16.0 GB of system memory, and a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps, with no local storage or GPU. Benchmark results consistently place this instance in the bottom 25% for CPU and memory performance, with a single-core stress-ng score of 1282.39 and a multi-core score of 3353.46. Redis SET operations perform in the bottom 10% at 1.44 million operations per second. Given its older hardware architecture and lower resource density, the m4.xlarge is qualitatively suited for legacy applications, basic web serving, and low-intensity development environments that require a stable, dedicated resource profile without demanding high computational throughput.
